description: Design inverting and non-inverting op-amp amplifiers and calculate gain from resistor ratios.
content_html:
The Operational Amplifier

An operational amplifier (op-amp) is an integrated circuit designed to amplify the difference between its two input voltages. It has an inverting input (marked “−”), a non-inverting input (marked “+”), and a single output. Without external components, its open-loop gain is enormous — typically hundreds of thousands — which makes it unstable for most applications. In practice, resistors are connected around the op-amp to form a negative feedback loop that sets a stable, predictable gain.

Two resistors define the gain in both configurations covered here: \(R_1\) (the input resistor, connected between the signal source and the op-amp input) and \(R_f\) (the feedback resistor, connected between the output and the inverting input). An important rule for your exam: both resistors must be at least 1 kΩ in any op-amp circuit design.

The Inverting Amplifier

In an inverting amplifier, the input signal is applied through \(R_1\) to the “−” input. The feedback resistor \(R_f\) connects from the output back to the same “−” input. The “+” input is connected to 0 V (ground).

Because the signal enters the inverting input, the output is 180° out of phase with the input — if the input goes positive, the output goes negative. The voltage gain is:

Key Fact

Inverting amplifier voltage gain:

$$G = -\frac{R_f}{R_1}$$

The negative sign indicates phase inversion. Only the magnitude \(|G| = R_f / R_1\) determines how much the voltage is multiplied.

The concept of a virtual earth helps explain why the formula works. Negative feedback forces the voltage at the inverting input to be essentially 0 V, even though that point is not connected directly to ground. This means that \(R_1\) and \(R_f\) share the same voltage reference at the inverting pin, and Kirchhoff’s current law gives the gain ratio.

An inverting amplifier uses \(R_1 = 10\) kΩ and \(R_f = 100\) kΩ. The input signal is a sine wave with a peak of 50 mV.

Step 1 — Calculate gain: \(G = -R_f / R_1 = -100 / 10 = -10\).

Step 2 — Calculate output peak: \(V_{OUT} = G \times V_{IN} = -10 \times 50\text{ mV} = -500\text{ mV}\).

The magnitude is 500 mV (0.5 V peak) and the output is inverted relative to the input. On a voltage–time graph, when the input sine wave is at its positive peak, the output is at its negative peak.

If you need to find \(R_f\) for a target gain: \(R_f = |G| \times R_1 = 10 \times 10 = 100\) kΩ. Always check that both resistors are ≥ 1 kΩ.

The Non-Inverting Amplifier

In a non-inverting amplifier, the input signal connects to the “+” input. The feedback network (\(R_f\) and \(R_1\)) connects from the output back to the “−” input, with \(R_1\) going from the inverting input to ground. The output is in phase with the input — positive input gives positive output.

Key Fact

Non-inverting amplifier voltage gain:

$$G = 1 + \frac{R_f}{R_1}$$

The “1 +” means the minimum gain is always greater than 1 (since \(R_f / R_1\) is positive). There is no phase inversion.

The non-inverting configuration is one of the least well answered topics in recent exams. The key distinction from the inverting case is: the input goes to the “+” pin and the feedback still goes to the “−” pin via \(R_f\). If you draw the circuit, \(R_1\) sits between the “−” pin and ground, and \(R_f\) connects the output back to that same “−” pin.

Design a non-inverting amplifier with a gain of 11. Choose \(R_1 = 10\) kΩ.

Rearrange: \(R_f = (G - 1) \times R_1 = (11 - 1) \times 10 = 100\) kΩ.

Check: \(G = 1 + R_f / R_1 = 1 + 100/10 = 1 + 10 = 11\). Correct. Both resistors are above 1 kΩ.

With \(V_{IN} = 100\) mV: \(V_{OUT} = 11 \times 0.1 = 1.1\) V. The output is in phase with the input (positive input gives positive output).

Comparing the Two Configurations

The table below summarises the key differences between the two op-amp circuits:

FeatureInvertingNon-inverting
Input connects to− pin (via R1)+ pin
Gain formula\(-R_f / R_1\)\(1 + R_f / R_1\)
Phase shift180° inversionNo inversion
Minimum gainCan be <1Always ≥1

In both circuits, the output cannot exceed the supply rail voltage. Always check for clipping when the calculated output is close to the supply voltage.
exam_tip_html: The non-inverting amplifier has been cited as the least-successfully answered question in recent exams. Practise drawing it from memory: signal to the “+” pin, \(R_1\) from the “−” pin to ground, \(R_f\) from output back to the “−” pin. Do not drop the negative sign from the inverting gain formula — the examiner expects to see \(G = -R_f / R_1\) and will penalise a positive answer. Both resistors must be ≥ 1 kΩ in any design question.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Inverting amplifier: input to the “−” pin via \(R_1\), feedback via \(R_f\); gain \(G = -R_f / R_1\); output is phase-inverted.
  • Non-inverting amplifier: input to the “+” pin; gain \(G = 1 + R_f / R_1\); output is in phase; minimum gain is always > 1.
  • Both resistors must be ≥ 1 kΩ in exam design questions; always check the output against supply rails to identify clipping.

practice_questions.text:
An inverting amplifier has R1 = 22 kΩ and Rf = 220 kΩ. What is its voltage gain?
A) −10
B) +10
C) −0.1
D) +22
State the difference in phase between the input and output of an inverting amplifier.
practice_questions.marks: The output is 180° out of phase with the input [1]; when the input is at a positive peak the output is at a negative peak [1].

practice_questions.text: A non-inverting amplifier is required with a voltage gain of 21. The designer chooses R1 = 10 kΩ. Calculate the value of Rf needed.
practice_questions.marks: \(R_f = (G - 1) \times R_1 = (21 - 1) \times 10 = 200\) kΩ [1 mark for correct rearrangement; 1 mark for correct answer with unit].

practice_questions.text:
A non-inverting amplifier has R1 = 47 kΩ and Rf = 470 kΩ. The input is a 200 mV peak sine wave and the supply is ±9 V.
(a) Calculate the voltage gain. [1 mark]
(b) Calculate the peak output voltage. [1 mark]
(c) State whether clipping will occur and explain why. [2 marks]
practice_questions.marks:
(a) \(G = 1 + 470/47 = 1 + 10 = 11\) [1].
(b) \(V_{OUT} = 11 \times 0.2 = 2.2\) V [1].
(c) Clipping will not occur [1] because 2.2 V is less than the ±9 V supply rails [1].

practice_questions.text: Describe how a non-inverting amplifier circuit is connected. Include the role of R1 and Rf in your answer.
practice_questions.marks: The input signal connects to the non-inverting (+) input of the op-amp [1]. R1 connects from the inverting (−) input to ground [1]. Rf connects from the output back to the inverting (−) input [1]. Together R1 and Rf form the negative feedback network that sets the gain to 1 + Rf/R1 [1].

practice_questions.text:
A student wants to amplify a sensor signal using an inverting amplifier. The sensor produces a peak signal of 80 mV and the system requires a peak output of 960 mV.
(a) Calculate the required voltage gain magnitude. [1 mark]
(b) The student chooses R1 = 10 kΩ. Calculate the value of Rf. [2 marks]
(c) The amplifier supply is ±12 V. The student then connects a sensor that occasionally produces peaks of 160 mV. Analyse whether the output will be clipped and justify your answer. [3 marks]
(d) Suggest one change to the circuit that would prevent clipping with the larger signal. [2 marks]
practice_questions.type: 8 marks — Extended Response: Circuit Analysis and Evaluation
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: All parts correct with clear working: (a) G = 960/80 = 12; (b) Rf = 12 × 10 = 120 kΩ; (c) at 160 mV input, output = 12 × 160 = 1920 mV = 1.92 V — within ±12 V supply, so no clipping; (d) valid change: increase supply voltage, reduce R1/Rf ratio to lower gain, or add an input attenuator.
Secure: Three parts correct; minor algebraic slip in one.
Developing: Gain and Rf calculated correctly; clipping analysis incomplete.
Emerging: Gain formula applied but Rf or clipping analysis incorrect.

knowledge_checks.q: In an inverting amplifier, where does the input signal connect?
options: To the inverting (−) input via R1

knowledge_checks.q: What is the gain formula for a non-inverting amplifier?
In a non-inverting amplifier, the minimum possible gain is always _____ than 1.
Negative feedback in an op-amp circuit connects the output back to the _____ input.
Match each configuration to its gain formula:
right: Inverting input held at approximately 0 V by feedback

flashcard_questions.q: What is the gain formula for an inverting op-amp amplifier?
What is the gain formula for a non-inverting op-amp amplifier?
In an inverting amplifier, the output is ___° out of phase with the input.
In a non-inverting amplifier, is the output in phase or out of phase with the input?
What is the minimum voltage gain of a non-inverting amplifier?
flashcard_questions.a: Greater than 1 (since Rf/R1 is always positive).

flashcard_questions.q: What is the virtual earth in an inverting op-amp circuit?
flashcard_questions.a: The inverting input, held at ~0 V by negative feedback despite not being grounded.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the minimum resistor value in an op-amp circuit design (exam rule)?
What is the voltage gain of an inverting amplifier with R1 = 10 kΩ and Rf = 47 kΩ?
A non-inverting amplifier needs a gain of 6. If R1 = 10 kΩ, what is Rf?
Where does the input signal connect in a non-inverting amplifier?
flashcard_questions.a: To the non-inverting (+) input of the op-amp.

flashcard_questions.q: What connects from the output back to the inverting (−) input in both op-amp configurations?

glossary_terms.definition: An integrated circuit with two inputs and one output, used as the building block of precision amplifier circuits.
A connection from the output of an amplifier back to its inverting input, used to set a stable, precise gain.

An op-amp circuit where the input signal connects to the inverting (−) input via R1 and the feedback resistor Rf connects from output to inverting input; the output is phase-inverted relative to the input.
The inverting input of an op-amp in a closed-loop circuit, which is held at approximately 0 V by the negative feedback even though it is not directly connected to ground.
An op-amp circuit where the input signal connects to the non-inverting (+) input; the output is in phase with the input and the gain is always greater than 1.
